page_title: The Conjoined Triangles of Senior-Level Development

sources.entry: The Conjoined Triangles of Senior-Level Development looks into how to define a senior engineer.

summary.title: The Conjoined Triangles of Senior-Level Development
summary.one_liner: Learn how one company defined "senior developer" using three tracks (technical capability, leadership, community) and why gut-feeling seniority judgments invite bias.
keywords: how long to become senior developer
takeaways: Seniority is hard to define; common definitions (years of experience, books, whiteboard algorithms) conflict and invite bias.
Frontside frames seniority as how much direction a person needs versus how much they can provide to others.
Seniority is assessed across three tracks: technical capability, leadership, and community/connectedness, with evidence (artifacts) for each.
A person can be senior on the technical track plus one other track; technical skill alone is not enough at their small company.
Becoming senior generally takes several years, and people with leadership or community skills can often catch up technically faster.
summary.summary: The author, Brandon Hays of Frontside, describes a company meeting where the team could not agree on what "senior developer" means while hiring. He argues that vague, gut-feeling definitions enable bias and title inflation, and that criteria need accountability. He explains Frontside's approach: derive responsibilities from its environment, then assess three tracks (technical, leadership, community) using concrete artifacts. The post is an opinion piece with examples rather than a step-by-step tutorial, and it promises a follow-up post with the 12 detailed traits.
